A video game is a waste of time. I say that as someone that plays a lot of them. But ultimately, if you are playing a video game, you are not being productive. The skills that you're refining aren't meaningful in any way. It's fun, but that's all it is. So remove the expectation - as others have said, if you're not enjoying yourself, turn it off. Remember, the point of a game is to take a break from the things that matter, not to become a thing that matters. Your value as a person is in no way tied to a K:D ratio - and that works either way - being really good at a game is a petty source of pride, it's not something that's worth aspiring to at the expense of your own enjoyment. In other words, some things are worth putting in hard work towards, even when you don't feel like it. A game isn't one of them.

What do you like about yourself? What are your real accomplishments? Those are the things you should be getting your sense of self-worth from, and the areas you should reserve your emotional investment for.

To become truly good at a competitive activity, it requires a competitive psychology. There are a number of things I found worked for me - I was top 10,000 in my region on Starcraft 2 and top 20,000 in the world, back when there were 2 million people on the ladder.

  1. Focus only on yourself. Do not focus on your opponents. There will always be players better than you. World champions who maintain their titles don't assume they are the best - they assume there's someone better hiding out there and they take every match seriously and train just like they did before they won their title. It is better to be concerned with becoming the best player you can be and not focusing on being better than others.

  2. Learn to win when you lose. Do not judge your success based on victory, judge your success on your ability to gain new skill and improve. The only "loss condition" is a situation where you fail to learn and get better.

  3. Similarly to #1, never look for things to blame for any failure or loss, other than your own actions and decisions. You and you alone are responsible for whether you win or lose. Force yourself to believe this even when there's valid concerns about latency, balance, or cheating. The "blame game" is a psychological trap that prevents people from improving at games they play for years because it allows them to ignore or deny their own shortcomings and never correct them. even when there are valid balance/fairness issues, playing like there are not and just focusing on ways to compensate for circumstances can only make you a better player.

  4. Humility. Cannot stress this one enough. There is nothing to be gained by convincing yourself that you are "the shit"". Conversely, adopting the view that you are "simply shit"', no matter how good you are, will keep you focused on constantly getting better and make it easier to accept losses. This is why most people get angry - they want to think they are good when they aren't, and when they lose it conflicts with their internal perspective.
